title: What happened when 6.8m people were told real Monet art was AI
content:
AI content is polarizing. When users spot that AI was used in art, backlash often follows. So, let’s run a quick experiment.
Take a look at the picture below. I just generated an image, in the style of a Monet painting, using AI. I used the latest AI models trained on the world’s best artwork. Have a look, and think about what makes this image inferior to a real Monet painting. Think about what you like and what you don’t like about it.
Now, what if I told you that I lied? The image is a real Monet. A few weeks back, X user SHLOMS performed the same exercise. Let’s talk about what happened.
Over 1,300 people responded to SHLOMS’s post with resoundingly similar feedback. Almost everyone who replied said this AI art was pure crap.
They said it lacked “coherent composition.” The colors were an “incoherent muddle.” Some said it was “trying too hard .”
Others called the image “obvious AI slop.” They called it “garbage” and “borked nonsense with no sense of space.” Users picked holes in every aspect of the painting. They questioned its lack of meaning and how AI art simply lacks the magical quality imbued by human creativity.
But there’s a problem … this Monet painting is real.
SHOLMS lied. It was their version of a social experiment. They took a real (much-loved) Monet painting, pretended it was an AI-generated image, and then gauged the reaction.
I’ll be honest. My gut reaction to the X post was the same. I immediately thought it was slop. I tried to spot flaws and thought the colors were dull. And it turns out that all of us do this.
When we think art is created by AI, we tend to dislike it. In fact, when we think anything took no effort to build, we dislike it.
We follow what Andrea Morales , Lonnie L. Ostrom Chair in Business and professor in the Department of Marketing at Arizona State University, calls an “effort heuristic.” In other words, if something took two seconds to generate, we’ll hate it. If it took 15 years of craft to perfect, we’ll love it.
In a 2005 study published in the Journal of Consumer Research , Morales found that people will generally reward actions that took a great deal of effort. The study followed 46 participants who were in the market for a new home. They were told to hire a real estate agent to help them search. The agent reviewed their preferences and put together a personalized list of 10 apartments.
However, 23 of the participants were told the agent “did everything manually and spent nine hours building the list.” The other 23 were told that ​“the agent used a computer program, spending only one hour on the list.”
In reality, the houses on both lists were identical. The real estate agent lied about how much time they spent on the search. It always took one hour.
But perception was swayed by the perceived effort. Participants who were told that the list took nine hours to create rated the houses 30.5% higher. We use effort as a proxy to measure quality — especially when quality is hard to measure.
So when 6.8 million people saw an image of a real Monet painting but thought it was AI-generated, they immediately called it slop.
This presents a tricky contradiction. We’re repeatedly told that to compete, we need to embrace AI. But the Morales study shows a different perspective.
If we only use AI (or even if people think we only use AI), people will feel an urge to hate our work. The fantastic copywriter Dave Harland calls this “ Death By Sepia .”
Taken from Dave’s “The Word” newsletter (sign up here ).
The landlord at the Bluebell might think this sign is infinitely better than a standard blackboard sign. They might say, “It’s colorful! It stands out! It includes all of our menu! Even a goblet of wine!”
But most people will see it and recognize that off-sepia tone as AI. And as we’ve seen with Monet, once people think something is lazily created with just AI, they’ll dislike it.
I spoke with Professor Matt Johnson about why some AI content falls flat on a recent episode of Nudge. Listen here.
AI changes the calculus of creation, but it doesn’t change human psychology. People still want to know that someone cared and put something of themselves into the work.
Your audience is doing the same math on everything you publish. Give them a reason to believe that someone put their time, effort, and craft into your marketing.

title: The State Of Search In 2026: Zero Click Searches At An All-Time High
content:
The latest Datos x SparkToro State of Search Report is out, and it’s something of a doozy. AI is certainly on the rise, search still hasn’t been replaced (it’s not even in the process of), and more people than ever stay in Google’s ecosystem .
Rather than read it in its entirety, you can watch or listen to me talk about it here:
Nothing hugely surprising of course. However, there are a couple of points that piqued my interest without making it into the headline findings.
Given the extraordinarily good state of Google’s revenues , I’m surprised to see such a significant reduction in paid clicks between March and June 2026. In the U.S., they dropped from 2.3% to 1.3% and in the EU/UK, 2.4% to 1.4%.
Maybe Google has decided now’s the time to try something novel given how strong their advertising revenue base is . This does also coincide with record levels of users that stay on Google, or click through to another Google-owned property:
Maybe they have expanded AI Overviews in more territories recently ( French rollout took place in July 2026 ), or given AI Mode a more significant push. We know these surfaces do not monetize as well advertising-wise as traditional interfaces.
This data corroborates in the EU/UK, but not in the U.S. One to hypothesize over.
In Europe, Wikipedia went from being the seventh most visited domain from search in Q2 2025 to the third most visited in Q2 2026.
This feels like the antithesis of what we’d expect to see – who visits websites anymore?
Some people obviously, which is encouraging. My only slight hunch is that users are looking for ways to corroborate the information they are ingesting at a furious rate from less reliable sources.
Or, I suppose, Wikipedia may be ranking more effectively.
Navigational searches fell hardest on smaller engines – Yahoo, DuckDuckGo, Bing, et al. – all saw more significant drops in navigational searches than Google’s 22.9% – 16.4% in the U.S. market.
But informational searches rose significantly. In the U.S. market, informational searches accounted for 59.69% in Q2 2025 compared to 65.12% in Q2 2026. The EU/UK saw a comparable rise over that same time period – 55.39% to 61.31%.
I’m not a statistician, but if this is based on share of search alone, then the “drop” in navigational searches could be down to the far more significant rise in informational searches.
We know that AI visibility has measurable downstream impact and that AI excels in the research phase. While search is becoming less valuable here, AI usage may be increasing subsequent informational searches in Google.
There is, of course, far more in the report around desktop usage, searches per user, query length to name but a few. But to me, these are the headlines.
